lead: An inner product takes two complex vectors and returns a complex number. It gives length, angle and orthogonality. A complex vector space with an inner product, and with no missing limit points, is a Hilbert space. Dirac notation writes a vector as a ket |ψ⟩ and its partner as a bra ⟨φ|. The bracket ⟨φ|ψ⟩ is the inner product. Quantum states, gates and measurements use this language, so it is the working notation of quantum computing.
prereq: You need: complex numbers and vector spaces; this chapter adds an inner product to that stage.

sections.h3: Inner product, norm and Hilbert space

blocks.text: Start with a vector space over the complex numbers C, as in 1.2. An inner product is a rule that takes an ordered pair (|φ⟩, |ψ⟩) and returns a complex number, written ⟨φ|ψ⟩. It must obey three rules.

items: Conjugate symmetry: ⟨ψ|φ⟩ = ⟨φ|ψ⟩*. The star means complex conjugate.
Linearity in the second slot: ⟨φ|aψ+bχ⟩ = a⟨φ|ψ⟩+b⟨φ|χ⟩ for complex numbers a and b.
Positive definite: ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ is real and ≥0, and equals 0 only for |ψ⟩=0.

blocks.text: Some books put linearity in the first slot; keep one convention and check the star.

blocks.where: ||ψ|| is the norm (length) of |ψ⟩; ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ is real and non-negative.

blocks.text: Two vectors are orthogonal when ⟨φ|ψ⟩=0. A vector is normalized when ||ψ||=1. A Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space: every Cauchy sequence of vectors converges to a vector in the space. In finite dimensions, Cⁿ is automatically complete, so every finite-dimensional complex inner-product space is a Hilbert space. That is enough for qubits and gates here; infinite dimensions need extra analysis.

Write a ket |ψ⟩ as a column vector of complex numbers. In C², |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩+β|1⟩, where α and β are complex coefficients. The computational basis is |0⟩=(1,0)ᵀ and |1⟩=(0,1)ᵀ. The symbol ᵀ means transpose.
The bra ⟨ψ| is the conjugate transpose: turn the column into a row and conjugate every entry. For |ψ⟩ above, ⟨ψ| = α*⟨0|+β*⟨1|. The bra is the dual partner of the ket.
For |φ⟩=γ|0⟩+δ|1⟩, the bracket is ⟨φ|ψ⟩ = γ*α+δ*β. This is one complex number, not a vector. Order matters: ⟨φ|ψ⟩ and ⟨ψ|φ⟩ are conjugates, not generally equal.
Measurement probabilities use |α|² and |β|²; see Unit 2, Quantum measurement.
A basis {|i⟩} is orthonormal when ⟨i|j⟩=δᵢⱼ: 1 if i=j, 0 if i≠j. Any vector expands as |ψ⟩ = Σᵢ cᵢ|i⟩. Taking the inner product with ⟨j| gives cⱼ=⟨j|ψ⟩, because only the j term survives.

blocks.where: I is the identity operator; the sum runs over every vector in an orthonormal basis; |i⟩⟨i| is an outer product.

blocks.text: Acting on |ψ⟩, the term |i⟩⟨i|ψ⟩ keeps the coefficient along |i⟩. The sum rebuilds |ψ⟩. This is why an orthonormal basis is a complete set of projectors. For a qubit, |0⟩⟨0|+|1⟩⟨1| gives I; inserting this sum anywhere does not change the state.

In C² the computational basis is one orthonormal basis. Other bases, such as the Hadamard basis in Unit 3, are equally valid. Coefficients change with the basis; the vector does not. Completeness is used whenever we insert a basis between operators.

examples.question: Let |ψ⟩ = (1/√2)|0⟩ + (i/√2)|1⟩ in C². (a) Find ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ and ||ψ||. (b) Find ⟨0|ψ⟩ and ⟨1|ψ⟩. (c) Check the coefficients using the orthonormal-basis rule.
steps: The coefficients are α=1/√2 and β=i/√2.
For an orthonormal basis, cᵢ=⟨i|ψ⟩. The values c₀=1/√2 and c₁=i/√2 match the given coefficients.
examples.answer: The state is normalized: ⟨ψ|ψ⟩=1 and ||ψ||=1. The inner products are ⟨0|ψ⟩=1/√2≈0.7071 and ⟨1|ψ⟩=i/√2≈0.7071 i.
examples.check:
import math
alpha = 1 / math.sqrt(2)
beta = 1j / math.sqrt(2)
norm_sq = abs(alpha)**2 + abs(beta)**2
print(round(norm_sq, 6))
print(round(alpha.real, 6))
print(round(beta.imag, 6))

traps: The bra is the conjugate transpose, not just the transpose. For |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1⟩, ⟨ψ|=α*⟨0|+β*⟨1|.
Reversing the order conjugates the bracket: ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩*. Do not swap the two vectors without the star.
The inner product is linear in the second slot and conjugate-linear in the first: ⟨aφ|bψ⟩=a*b⟨φ|ψ⟩.
The norm is √⟨ψ|ψ⟩, not ⟨ψ|ψ⟩. Measurement uses squared modulus |α|², which is not the same as α.
The completeness relation Σ|i⟩⟨i|=I holds for an orthonormal basis, not for an arbitrary list of vectors.

quiz.q: Write |0⟩ and |1⟩ as column vectors and state their inner products.
Define a Hilbert space and list the three inner-product rules.
quiz.a: A Hilbert space is a complete complex inner-product space. The rules are conjugate symmetry ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩*, linearity in the second slot, and positive definiteness ⟨ψ|ψ⟩≥0 with equality only for |ψ⟩=0.

quiz.q: Why is the bra called the conjugate transpose of the ket?
quiz.a: A ket is a column vector. The bra is the row vector obtained by transposing it and conjugating every entry. This makes the bracket ⟨φ|ψ⟩ equal to the matrix product of row ⟨φ| and column |ψ⟩.
The computational basis is orthonormal, so ⟨0|0⟩=1 and ⟨0|1⟩=0. Taking ⟨0| against α|0⟩+β|1⟩ leaves α.

quiz.q: Using completeness Σ|i⟩⟨i|=I, show cⱼ=⟨j|ψ⟩ for |ψ⟩=Σ cᵢ|i⟩.
quiz.a: Take ⟨j|ψ⟩=⟨j|Σᵢ cᵢ|i⟩=Σᵢ cᵢ⟨j|i⟩. Orthonormality gives ⟨j|i⟩=δⱼᵢ, so only i=j survives. Hence ⟨j|ψ⟩=cⱼ.

quiz.q: A student writes ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩. Correct it and give the rule with an example.
quiz.a: The correct rule is ⟨ψ|φ⟩=⟨φ|ψ⟩*. Example: if ⟨φ|ψ⟩=1/2−i/2, then ⟨ψ|φ⟩=1/2+i/2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces appear in functional analysis and in quantum field theory, where states are wavefunctions or operators on a space of functions. Quantum information usually stays in finite dimensions, because a register of n qubits lives in C^(2^n). The completeness relation is the algebraic workhorse behind basis changes, measurement projectors and channel representations.
